wine.name: Scharzhofberger Riesling Spätlese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Spätlese: late picked, at least 76 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, part of it from ungrafted vines planted more than a century ago.
wine.sites: The Scharzhofberg, the steep south facing hill of grey slate above the Scharzhof at Wiltingen, in the cold Saar valley; the estate farms its share from the house at its foot.
wine.making: The hill is picked in several selective passes, so that each Prädikat is a true selection. The juice ferments slowly with wild yeasts in traditional thousand litre oak Fuder casks in the deep cellar of the Scharzhof, and the fermentation is stopped with natural sugar left behind, the wine low in alcohol and high in acid.
wine.glass: White peach, apricot and lime blossom over wet slate and green apple; the sugar reads as texture rather than sweetness against a piercing Saar acidity, and age adds honey, quince and smoke.
wine.ageing: Delicious young for its fruit, it then closes for some years, and a strong vintage keeps for thirty years and more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with crab, pork cooked with fruit, or on its own.

label.means: The vineyard, an Ortsteil, printed without the village name Wiltingen.
Late picked, at least 76 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel; here naturally sweet.
The wine region, named Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007; the Saar lies within it.

records.table: Low in alcohol and naturally sweet, Egon Müller's Scharzhofberger Riesling Spätlese grows on the steep grey slate hill above the Scharzhof in the cold Saar valley. Peach and apricot sit over slate, and the acid is so high that the sugar reads as texture.
records.story: Through the Middle Ages the Scharzhof and its hill belonged to a monastery of Trier, and the slope was planted with vines long before any Müller lived there. When the French, who then held the land, took church property and sold it, the estate went to auction in 1797, and a forebear of the family bought it; his descendants, the Müllers among them, have kept it since. Several heads of the house carried the name Egon, so the label names a line rather than one man. Germany's wine law of 1971 fixed the Prädikat ladder of Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese that the labels follow, and in 2007 the region's name, Mosel-Saar-Ruwer, was shortened to Mosel. Through those changes the estate held to sweet wine of very low alcohol and very high acid, fermented with wild yeasts in Fuder casks and picked in several passes so that each Prädikat is a true selection. Lots of its Auslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are sold at the Trier auction of the Grosser Ring, the association of the Mosel's auction estates founded there in 1908. A candidate who knows the Spätlese knows the Saar's measure, the hill and the hand of the auction wines in a frame a table can share.

Several growers own parcels of the Scharzhofberg, so the vineyard name alone does not mean Egon Müller.
The Saar is a part of the Mosel region, not a region of its own.

report: Rechecked with seven searches of its own and one shared on 12 November 2026; the estate's own site gave only its contact page, so the facts beyond the library rest on two secondary sources each or on the VDP, listed in reviews/recheck-mosel.json.

Confirmed: the auction of 1797 after the secularisation and the purchase by a forebear (Primum Familiae Vini and wein.plus), the monastery of Trier, the ungrafted vines (Falstaff, Westgarth and a merchant), wild yeasts and old thousand litre Fuder casks (Westgarth and the Sommelier Academy), the Grosser Ring of 1908 at Trier (the VDP and wein.plus).

Changed: the auction is no longer called the September auction, since the VDP held it in November 2025 and moves it to the spring; the card no longer calls Scharzberg one letter away; the region's name was shortened in 2007, the Saar did not join it then.
Taken out for want of a source: the cold of the cellar stopping the fermentation (one source has it stopped with sulphur), the rest on the lees through winter and the spring bottling.
The buyer of 1797 (Jean-Jacques or Jakob Koch) and the Müller marriage of 1837 are left unnamed and undated: the dates of the buyer were found nowhere and the marriage in one source only.
The head of the house is living and is not named; the house keeps its name, which is his and his forebears'.
The plan's note asked for Spätlese or Auslese; Spätlese is taught as the wine a guest meets, with the Auslese and the Kabinett among the others.

changed: grapes: part of the fruit from ungrafted vines planted more than a century ago, by Falstaff and Westgarth, where it said some of them on their own roots with no source.

making: wild yeasts in traditional thousand litre oak Fuder casks in the deep cellar and a stopped fermentation, by Westgarth and the Sommelier Academy; the cold of the cellar, the lees through winter and the spring bottling cut for want of a source.

story: the auction of 1797 bought by a forebear whose descendants kept it, by Primum Familiae Vini and wein.plus, where it said the estate passed to the family; the region renamed in 2007 rather than the Saar joining it; its rarest lots now lots of its Auslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, and the September of the auction cut as volatile, the VDP having held it in November 2025 and moving it to the spring.

wine.name: Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Auslese: selected bunches, at least 83 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from the blue slate of the Sonnenuhr.
wine.sites: The Wehlener Sonnenuhr, a steep slope of blue Devonian slate across the river from Wehlen, named for the sundial set in its rock in 1842.
wine.making: Selected bunches, ripe and often touched by noble rot, are picked by hand and kept apart for the Auslese. The juice ferments cool with wild yeasts, mostly in stainless steel with a few old wooden casks as the year decides, and rests long on its lees; the fermentation is stopped with natural sugar left, and the young wine keeps a reductive, struck match smell and a faint prickle.
wine.glass: In youth struck match and smoke over white peach and lime, with a faint prickle; with age honey, candied apricot, quince and slate, sweet yet weightless and lifted by bright acidity.
wine.ageing: Often unapproachable for years, it opens after ten and keeps for several decades, turning to honey and smoke.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly so the struck match can clear; a white wine glass.

label.means: The sundial vineyard of Wehlen; the village comes first, with er added.
Selected bunches at a legal minimum ripeness, often with noble rot; sweet.
A gold capsule, named on a list, for a richer selection of the same Prädikat; a long gold capsule richer again.

records.table: Expect struck match when a young JJ Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese is opened: the house's sweet wines from the blue slate slope named for its sundial need years. With age they turn to honey and smoke while staying light on the tongue.
records.story: The sundial that names the Sonnenuhr was set in the slate across the river from Wehlen in 1842 by a member of the Prüm family. In 1911 the family estate was divided among heirs, and one of them founded the estate whose label carries his name in short. His son worked there from 1920 and led it until his death in 1969, and he is credited with the style it is known by: light, sweet wines, fermented with wild yeasts and stopped with natural sugar, that smell of struck match when young and seem closed for years. Germany's wine law of 1971 set the Prädikat names on the labels; within them the house marks a richer Auslese with a gold capsule and a richer one again with a long gold capsule. Other Prüm estates share the name and the village, which keeps guests and candidates alert. The estate's fame rests on sweet wines that a patient cellar turns into honey and smoke over decades. Two habits come with it: read the village before the vineyard, and look at the capsule as well as the print.

The struck match and the prickle of a young bottle are the house's signature, not a fault.
Sonnenuhr means sundial and appears at Wehlen, Zeltingen and Brauneberg, so the village name carries the answer.

report: Rechecked with five searches on 12 November 2026; the estate has no history page a search returned, so every fact beyond the library rests on two secondary sources, listed in reviews/recheck-mosel.json.

Confirmed: the division of 1911 among the heirs (Wikipedia, wein.plus, Falstaff), the son at the estate from 1920 and dead in 1969 and the style credited to him, wild yeasts and a cool fermentation mostly in steel with a few old casks by the year, long lees, the struck match of youth (Decanter, CellarTracker), the sundial of 1842 (the Codex and wein.plus) and the two capsules marking riper Auslese lots (two merchants).
Changed: the founder is one of the heirs, not the son who took his share; the son's style is told as the wine, not as late picking; the vessels are now given.

Taken out for want of a source: much of the fruit from old vines, the sundial set so that workers could tell the time, picking late as the son's rule, and the Kabinett as the hardest wine to make well, a judgement.

The founder (Johann Josef Prüm, 1873 to 1944 in one source only), his son (Sebastian Prüm, 1902 to 1969 in one source, his age at death in another) and the sundial's maker (Jodocus Prüm, 1807 to 1876 in one source) are described; the living family is not named.
The library's trap calls the other Prüm estates unrelated; S.A. Prüm is a branch of the same family by Wikipedia and wein.plus, so the record says only that several Prüm estates share the name.
Auslese is taught for the capsule lesson, the Auslese Goldkapsel being the Prüm wine on the house list, with the Spätlese and Kabinett among the others.

changed: grapes: much of it from old vines cut, found in no source; the blue slate of the Sonnenuhr is the library's.

making: hand picked selected bunches kept apart, a cool fermentation with wild yeasts mostly in stainless steel with a few old wooden casks as the year decides and long lees, by Decanter and CellarTracker, where it named no vessel.

wine.name: Erdener Prälat Riesling Auslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein: Auslese, the selected harvest, 83 degrees Oechsle at least on the Mosel
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from old vines on their own roots, some of them a century old.
wine.sites: The Prälat, a small, steep, rocky slope of red slate across the river from the village of Erden, facing south and sheltered between the river and a massif of rock; it is counted the warmest site of the Mittelmosel.
wine.making: Selected bunches, many touched by noble rot, which the sheltered site gives in most years by the estate's account, ferment spontaneously with wild yeasts in large old oak casks. The fermentation stops with natural sugar left behind, and the wine stays on its lees, unstirred, for about a year before bottling.
wine.glass: Ripe apricot, candied orange peel and blood orange over smoke, ginger and red slate, with honey and saffron; rich and concentrated, yet carried by bright acidity to a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy within five years, it gains depth for twenty and keeps for decades.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass and a modest pour, with blue cheese or a fruit tart.

label.means: The Prälat vineyard of Erden; the village name comes first.

records.table: Old ungrafted vines on a steep red slate slope between rock and river, counted the warmest site of the Mittelmosel, give Dr. Loosen's Erdener Prälat Riesling Auslese. It is rich and sweet, apricot and blood orange over smoke and ginger, yet bright.
records.story: Around Bernkastel the Loosens have owned vines for more than two centuries, by the family's own account, and over that time they gathered parcels in the steep slopes downriver: the Würzgarten at Ürzig and the Treppchen and the Prälat at Erden. The Prälat was part of the Treppchen until it was marked out as a site of its own at the end of the nineteenth century, and it was named in honour of a prelate and professor from Ürzig, a grower's son. Its red slate between rock and water makes it the warm heart of that stretch of the river, and the family's vines there grow on their own roots. In 1988 a son of the family took over the estate and set out to carry Mosel Riesling back onto the wine lists of the world; the estate joined the VDP in 1993. That work took it beyond the valley. In 1999 it made the first Eroica Riesling with Chateau Ste. Michelle of Washington State, and it also took on an estate in the Pfalz. The Prälat Auslese stayed at the centre of the range as its most concentrated wine. Set beside a Wehlen wine, it shows the other face of the slate, red rock and warmth, orange and ginger where blue slate gives peach and lime.

Erdener Prälat and Erdener Treppchen are two different vineyards of the same village; the Prälat was marked out of the Treppchen late in the nineteenth century.

wine.name: Bernkasteler Doctor Riesling Spätlese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, the Spätlese rung: grapes picked late, 76 degrees Oechsle at least here
wine.sites: The Bernkasteler Doctor, a small, steep slope directly above the town of Bernkastel, facing south south west at gradients up to 70 per cent: dark, rocky, weathered Devonian slate rich in fine earth, planted mostly with ungrafted Riesling.
wine.making: Picked by hand in several selective passes, the grapes are pressed and the juice ferments with its own wild yeasts, in stainless steel or in oak casks as the year and the lot decide; the fermentation is stopped to keep natural sweetness.
wine.glass: Smoke and apple skin over white peach, lemon and grey slate; dense and upright, with the Doctor's weight behind a firm acidity and a sweetness that reads lighter than it is.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed for five years or more, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty and longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with smoked trout or roast pork.

label.means: The old spelling of Bernkasteler Doctor that the house keeps on its labels: the Doctor vineyard of Bernkastel.

records.table: Thanisch has held a share of the Bernkasteler Doctor, the steep slate slope right above the town, since the nineteenth century, and its Spätlese is the house's classic reading of the site. Smoky and dense, apple and peach, it is sweet but stands upright.
records.story: The legend of the Doctor is set in 1360: an Archbishop of Trier, lying ill with a fever at Landshut castle above Bernkastel, was brought wine from this slope and recovered, and he named it the true doctor. The vineyard has carried the name since. The Thanisch family has grown vines on the Middle Mosel since the first half of the seventeenth century, by its own account, and it came to hold a share of the Doctor in the nineteenth. The head of the family, a doctor by degree and a member of the Prussian parliament, died in 1895 at forty one; his widow took charge with three small children, and her title stayed on the label: Wwe., short for Witwe, before Dr. H. Thanisch. By the estate's account she was among the founders of the Grosser Ring, the Mosel's auction estates, in 1908. In 1988 the family divided its holdings between heirs, and two estates came to bear the name, Erben Thanisch and Erben Müller-Burggraef, each with its own part of the Doctor. The Spätlese is the house's classic reading of the site: smoky, dense and firm. Read the long name to the end, then, since the heirs and not the widow tell you which house made the wine.

wine.name: Maximin Grünhäuser Abtsberg Riesling Kabinett
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Kabinett: the lightest rung, at least 70 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel
wine.sites: The Abtsberg, the abbot's hill, first in rank of the estate's three hills: a rounded hill of blue Devonian slate on the steep south facing side of the Ruwer valley at Mertesdorf, with slopes as steep as 75 per cent.
wine.making: After pressing and settling, the juice ferments only with wild yeasts, in thousand litre oak Fuder casks or small steel tanks, in the estate's historic cellar; the fermentation ends with a gentle natural sweetness left in the wine.
wine.glass: Green apple, lime and blackcurrant leaf over wet slate, with a hint of white peach; feather light, racy and long, its gentle sweetness reading almost dry against the Ruwer's acidity.
wine.ageing: Bright and charming young, a good Abtsberg Kabinett keeps and gains for ten to twenty years.
wine.serve: 7 to 9 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, as an aperitif or with river trout.

label.means: The estate's name standing in place of a village, as an Ortsteil does, before each vineyard.

records.table: Abtsberg means the abbot's hill, first in rank of the three hills of Maximin Grünhaus, an estate on the Ruwer once held by the Benedictine abbey of St Maximin at Trier. Feather light, green apple and blackcurrant leaf over blue slate, its Riesling Kabinett tastes nearly dry.
records.story: The Grünhaus first appears in writing in 966, when an imperial charter confirmed a gift that a Frankish king had made in the seventh century to the Benedictine abbey of St Maximin at Trier, and the abbey's monks worked its slopes for centuries. Its three hills take their names from the abbey's order of rank: the Abtsberg the abbot's, the Herrenberg the lords', the Bruderberg the brothers'. In 1811, under Napoleon's secularisation, the estate was sold at auction to its first lay owner, a baron, and it passed through another family before 1882, when a baron of the Stumm family bought it; his daughter brought it to the von Schubert family as her dowry on her marriage. The three vineyards, each a monopole of the estate, are printed under the estate's own name, Maximin Grünhäuser, which German law treats as an Ortsteil standing in place of a village. The Ruwer is a small, cool side valley, and its wines are delicate, scented with herbs and blackcurrant leaf. The Abtsberg is the estate's first wine in rank, and its Kabinett the lightest way to meet it: in three names the estate keeps the order in which an abbey ranked its own hills.

questions.exp: Maximin Grünhäuser is an Ortsteil, an estate with village standing, so it stands in place of a village; the Abtsberg is a single vineyard, not a blend or a Grosslage.

questions.q: In which year does Maximin Grünhaus first appear in writing, in a charter confirming it to the abbey of St Maximin at Trier?
questions.exp: A charter of 966 is the first record; 1811 is its sale at auction under Napoleon, 1882 its purchase by the Stumm family and 1136 the founding of Kloster Eberbach in the Rheingau.

report: The house is not in the library. Rechecked with five searches on 12 November 2026; the estate's own pages on maximingruenhaus.de were read through search summaries, and every fact beyond the Codex rests on them, listed in reviews/recheck-mosel.json.

Confirmed: the charter of 966 by Otto I confirming a gift of King Dagobert I of the seventh century to the abbey of St Maximin, the three monopoles named for the abbey's ranks, the Abtsberg on blue Devonian slate with slopes to 75 per cent, the upper Herrenberg on red slate, wild yeasts only for the Kabinetts, Fuder casks or small steel tanks in the historic cellar.

Changed: the plan's 1882 was a purchase by Carl Ferdinand Freiherr von Stumm-Halberg, whose daughter brought the estate to the von Schubert family as her dowry, by the estate's own timeline; the sale under Napoleon is dated 1811, to a Freiherr von Handel, before the von Solemacher family.

Taken out for want of a source: the three walled slopes (the estate speaks of three monopoles, and no source read calls them walled), the vaulted cellar below the house, hand picking, the spring bottling and the Herrenberg as broader than the Abtsberg.
Otto I, Dagobert I, the barons of 1811 and 1882, the daughter and her husband are described rather than named, for want of dates sought in two sources; the living family is not named.
founded stays empty: 966 is a first record, not a founding, and 1882 a purchase.
The plan names no Prädikat for this house; Kabinett is taught as the lightest reading of the Abtsberg and the one Kabinett of the group.
